title: BOK article — reference knowledge about a subject
description:
Governs the YAML frontmatter of content/bok/<domain>/<slug>.md. An article explains a SUBJECT. It carries no proficiency levels, no role targets and no anchors, because those are claims about a PERSON and belong to the competence system. The two were originally one file and that produced neither a usable encyclopedia nor a clean assessment model — see decision 38 in docs/00-context.md.

Articles are sized by subject coherence, not by the taxonomy: one article may serve five elements and one element may draw on three articles. What makes that mapping precise is the SECTION. Every section carries a stable id, an element points at the specific section covering it, and the validator checks the link resolves.

THE USE CASE THIS EXISTS FOR: someone who demonstrated competence eight months ago and has forgotten a specific detail must be able to land on the documentation covering THAT detail, not on an article vaguely about the area with it buried inside. Retraining is not a realistic answer for a working practitioner.

Section ids therefore inherit the append-only discipline. Rename one and the refresher path silently dies for exactly the person who most needs it — the same failure mode as renaming an element ID, one layer down.

title.description: Names the subject, not the competence. 'Correlation and covariance in uncertainty budgets', not 'Constructing a budget with a correlated pair'.

subjects.description: Which domains this article informs. An array because subject matter does not respect the taxonomy: correlation belongs to uncertainty and to statistics at once, and duplicating the explanation into both would guarantee they diverge.

summary.description: What the article covers and what it is for. Shown in search results and at the top of the rendered page.

sections.description: The article's addressable structure. Declared here rather than inferred from the Markdown so the ids are explicit, reviewable in a diff, and cannot drift when someone rewords a heading. The validator checks every declared section has a matching {#id} anchor in the body and that nothing in the body is undeclared.

id.description: Stable within the article, and APPEND-ONLY. Sections may be added; an id already published must never be reused for different content, because an element's knowledgeRef and a reader's bookmark both resolve through it.

covers.description: What a reader will actually find here, in one line. Written for the person arriving cold from a credential eight months later, not for the author.

consensus.description:
Do competent practitioners AGREE about this? A separate axis from `currency.authorityStatus`, which answers what STANDING a claim has — where it comes from and whether it binds. The two are genuinely orthogonal and must not be collapsed: an ISO clause can be fully normative and its interpretation still contested, which in metrology is common rather than exotic.

Recorded per section rather than per article because disagreement attaches to a specific claim, not to a whole subject. Most sections are `established` and the field can be omitted.

The purpose is intellectual honesty. An encyclopedia that silently picks one side of a live professional disagreement and presents it as settled has overstated what the field knows, and has quietly substituted its authors' judgement for the profession's.

contestedBasis.description:
WHERE the disagreement lives, and therefore what would settle it. REQUIRED by the validator whenever consensus is `contested`. `consensus` says practitioners disagree; this says why, and the four cases are not interchangeable to a reader deciding what to do next.

`source-silent` — nothing authoritative reaches the question, so a laboratory must take a defensible position and record it. Includes the case where two sources each supply a method and neither says which to prefer. `source-ambiguous` — the statement at issue admits more than one honest reading, so the argument is about interpretation and an assessor may hold a view. The statement need not be a registered source: a manufacturer's specification describing a limit and a typical performance at once is the commonest instance in this corpus. `source-conflicting` — one source says two things that do not reconcile, so citing it settles nothing and a reader must be told so explicitly. `practice-diverges` — the source is clear and a substantial body of practice does otherwise, which is the one case where following the source is unremarkable and departing from it needs justifying.

The distinction is operational, not decorative, and it feeds the review trigger of open decision 12. A section contested because its source contradicts itself, or admits two readings, is exactly what a revision of that source might resolve — so it should wake when the source is revised. A section contested because no source reaches the question would NOT be resolved by a revision, and waking it on one wastes the reviewer. Collapsing the four loses the ability to tell those apart.

contestedBasisNote.description: Why THAT basis and not another — normally one or two sentences naming the clause that is silent, ambiguous or self-conflicting, or the practice that departs from it. Optional, and worth writing on every contested section: the enum on its own cannot be told apart from a value someone picked quickly, which is the same defect the `reviewedBy` pair on the ceiling plan exists to close.

alternativeViews.description: The other readings, stated in their strongest form. REQUIRED by the validator whenever consensus is contested, jurisdiction-dependent or organization-specific: a section flagged as disputed with no alternative recorded is worse than no flag at all, because it tells a reader there is controversy without telling them what it is, and leaves them less able to act than before.

position.description: What the alternative view holds. Write it as its holders would, not as a straw man — the same standard the L4/L5 assessment rubrics apply to a candidate.

basis.description: Why it is held. A position with no reasoning is a rumour.

heldBy.description: Where this view is found — a sector, a national practice, a school of thought. Not usually a named individual.

deprecated.description: The section is superseded but retained, because content is created and not destroyed. A reader following an old reference must still land somewhere that tells them what changed.

supersededBy.description: Where the reader should go instead.

citations.description: Referenceability is universal and applies to the BOK exactly as it applies to elements. An article with no clause-level citation is an opinion.

quotes.description: Tier-gated exactly as on an element. The BOK is the redistributable half of the project, so quotation limits matter MORE here than anywhere else.

currency.description: Knowledge ages on a different trigger from competence expectations, which is one of the reasons the two are now separate files. A revised edition of a standard should wake up every article tracking it without touching a single element.

authorityStatus.description: What STANDING this content has: where it comes from and whether it binds. Distinct from a section's `consensus`, which answers whether practitioners agree. Do not use one to express the other — a normative clause whose reading is contested is `authorityStatus: normative` with a contested section, not `authorityStatus: interpretation`.

authoring.description: Who made this and who looks after it. Structured rather than free-form because an encyclopedia that looks authoritative must be able to say where its content came from.

maintainer.description: Who is responsible for keeping it current. An article with a volatility of `volatile` and no maintainer is a liability.

reviews.description:
Technical review provenance. NOT a status flag — there is deliberately no `authoritative: true` field anywhere, because an article asserting its own authority is exactly the 'trust me' problem this project exists to solve. Authority is DERIVED from who reviewed the article, in what capacity, and what they concluded. A reader weighs the reviewers, as they would weigh the signers on a credential.

This also exists so that named external review does not disappear into git history. 'Reviewed by X, technical scope, accepted with changes, 2026-11' is auditable knowledge infrastructure; a commit log is not.

reviewType.description: Technical review says the metrology is right. Educational review says it can be learned from. Editorial says it reads well. They are different competencies and conflating them lets a copy-edit masquerade as a technical endorsement.

disposition.description: `disputed` is a legitimate and valuable outcome, not a failure state: a reviewer who disagrees on substance has told a reader something worth knowing, and suppressing it would make the encyclopedia less honest than the field it documents.

covers.description: WHICH SECTIONS WERE ACTUALLY REVIEWED, pinned by content. Scoped rather than whole-article because articles grow: a reviewer who read four sections in 2026 has not endorsed a fifth added in 2028, and an unscoped review would silently claim they had. The content pin makes a later rewrite detectable, so a review cannot keep vouching for prose its reviewer never saw.

note.description: Required when the disposition is `disputed` or `rejected`. A disagreement with no stated substance is unusable to a reader and unfair to the author.

conflictDisclosed.description: Any commercial or professional interest the reviewer disclosed, per GOVERNANCE.md. Recorded on the article rather than in a side channel, because a reader weighing the review needs it.
